UE26MA141A Engineering Mathematics – I · Unit 1 · Partial Differentiation

Introduction to Partial Differentiation

Complete study pack for class 001: functions of several variables, limits and continuity of a function of two variables, the definition and notation of partial derivatives, and second-order and mixed partial derivatives
Compiled from the PESU class 001 slide deck, its two AV-summary transcripts, the Unit 1 class-work sheet and past ESA papers. Generated 15 October 2026.

·How to use this pack

Class 001 has one deck and two recorded lectures: “Introduction to Partial Differentiation” (topics 1–2) and “Continuity and differentiability of a function of two independent variables” (topics 3–5). Topics 1–3 are the background (functions of two variables, limits, continuity) and are never asked by themselves in the ESA; topics 4–5 (computing partial derivatives and mixed partials) are used in every Unit 1 question. The geometrical interpretation and the problems on higher-order partials announced at the end of the second lecture are class 002, a separate pack. Every topic has the same parts: overview, key terms, formulas, figures, flowcharts, important points, worked examples, past-paper questions and a recap. IDs are shared with the separate documents: E = formula, G = graph, F = flowchart, W = worked example. Each ID is numbered by topic, so E4.2 is the second formula of topic 4.

1Functions of two or more variables

Most quantities depend on more than one variable: the area of a rectangle on its length and breadth, the volume of a cylinder on r and h, a potential on x,y,z,t. A function of two variables z=f(x,y) assigns to each ordered pair (x,y) in a domain D a unique real number. Its graph is a surface in three dimensions, so tools are used to plot it; this unit works with two variables, and everything extends to n variables.

Key terms and definitions

Function of two variables. A function of two variables denoted by z=f(x,y) is a rule that assigns to each ordered pair of real numbers (x,y) in a set D a unique real number denoted by f(x,y). The set D is the domain of f and its range is the set of values that f takes on: {f(x,y):(x,y)∈D}. S001·8 · T001a 00:05:46
Independent and dependent variables. In z=f(x,y), x and y are independent variables and z is the dependent variable (a bivariate function); with three independent variables one writes w=f(x,y,z), and in general f(x1​,x2​,…,xn​). transcript only T001a 00:02:18 · T001a 00:02:54

2Limit of a function of two variables

In one variable x can approach a only from the left or the right. In the plane (x,y) can approach (a,b) along infinitely many paths: lines, parabolas, ellipses. The limit is L only if every path gives L. Proving a limit exists is hard; proving it does not exist is easy: find two paths that give different values.

Key terms and definitions

Limit of a function of two variables. A function f(x,y) is said to approach the limit L as (x,y) approaches (a,b), if the limit remains the same along any path of (x,y) approaching (a,b): lim(x,y)→(a,b)​f(x,y)=L. S001·9 · T001a 00:11:01

Important points and why

  1. One variable: x→a from the left or the right only. Two variables: (x,y)→(a,b) along any of infinitely many paths (Figure G2.1). ESA ★ S001·9 · T001a 00:11:32 · T001a 00:12:34
  2. If substitution gives a number (a polynomial, no 00​), that number is the limit, whatever the path. ESA ★ T001a 00:13:59
  3. It is hard to show that a limit exists but easy to show it does not: two paths with different values are enough. ESA ★★ S001·10 · T001a 00:17:42
  4. Agreement along a few paths proves nothing: for 3x2+y22xy​, the x-axis and the parabola y=x2 both give 0, but y=x gives 21​. ESA ★★ T001a 00:16:48 · T001a 00:17:24
Why can one path never prove that a limit exists?
There are infinitely many paths, and a function can agree on any finite number of them and still differ on another: 3x2+y22xy​ gives 0 on the x-axis and on y=x2 but 21​ on y=x. To prove existence one needs an estimate for all paths at once (e.g. polar coordinates: x2+y23x2y​=3rcos2θsinθ→0).
added for clarityT001a 00:17:42 · S001·12
Exam trap. Same value along two or three paths does not prove that the limit exists; different values along two paths does prove it does not. T001a 00:16:48 · T001a 00:17:42
Exam trap. Slide 001·9 uses the point (2,1) (limit −8); the lecture uses (2,−1) (limit −6). Read the point in the question. added for clarity S001·9 · T001a 00:12:59

3Continuity of a function of two variables

f is continuous at (a,b) when f(a,b) is defined, the limit exists, and lim(x,y)→(a,b)​f(x,y)=f(a,b), as in one variable. Geometrically the surface has no hole or break there. A function can fail to be continuous even though the limit exists (x2+y23x2y​ at the origin), or because the limit does not exist (3x2+y22xy​).

Key terms and definitions

Continuity at a point. f(x,y) is continuous at (a,b) if lim(x,y)→(a,b)​f(x,y)=f(a,b): f(a,b) must be defined, the limit must exist, and the two must be equal. S001·11 · T001b 00:00:38 · T001a 00:18:46
“A function is continuous at a point if the graph doesn't have any holes or breaks at that point. Graphing the function is helpful. If a function is not continuous at (a,b), this does not mean the limit does not exist. We will need to consider the approaching (a,b) from different paths.” S001·11

Formulas

E3.1 · Continuity at (a, b)ESA ★
(x,y)→(a,b)lim​f(x,y)=f(a,b)
givesThe test for continuity.appliesThree conditions: f(a,b) defined, limit exists, both equal.noteOne variable: limx→c​f(x)=f(c).
S001·11 · T001b 00:00:38

Graphs and diagrams

Flowcharts

Important points and why

  1. One variable: f is continuous at c if (i) limx→c​f(x) exists, (ii) f(c) exists, (iii) they are equal. The same three conditions define continuity for f(x,y). ESA ★ T001a 00:18:46 · S001·11
  2. x2+y23x2y​: the limit at the origin exists (it is 0) but f(0,0) is 00​, so f is not continuous there. 3x2+y22xy​: the limit does not exist and f(0,0) is undefined (Figures G3.1–G3.2). ESA ★ S001·12 · S001·13 · T001b 00:04:14 · T001b 00:05:44
  3. To decide continuity in higher dimensions, graph the function: a hole, fold or sudden drop in the surface shows a discontinuity. ESA ★ S001·11 · T001b 00:06:45 · T001a 00:18:07
Why is x2+y23x2y​ not continuous at the origin even though its limit is 0?
Continuity needs f(0,0) to be defined and equal to the limit. Here f(0,0) is 00​, so the third condition cannot be checked. Defining f(0,0)=0 would make it continuous.
added for clarityS001·12 · T001b 00:04:14
Exam trap. “Not continuous” does not mean “the limit does not exist” (slide 001·11): x2+y23x2y​ has limit 0 at the origin. S001·11 · T001b 00:02:10
Exam trap. Continuous is not the same as smooth: z=∣x∣+∣y∣ is continuous everywhere but has a corner at the origin. The lecture's “continuous if the surface is smooth” is loose. added for clarity T001b 00:06:26

givenDiscuss the continuity of f(x,y)=x2+y23x2y​ at the origin.
step 1f(0,0)=00​ is not defined, so condition (ii) fails: f is not continuous at (0,0).
step 2The limit exists: in polar form x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ, f=3rcos2θsinθ, and ∣f∣≤3r→0 for every path (added for clarity).
step 3So lim(x,y)→(0,0)​f=0.

checksympy: polar form 3rsinθcos2θ.
S001·12 · T001b 00:02:41 · T001b 00:04:27
W3.2 · Limit does not exist, function not continuous (slide 001·13)ESA ★

short-note recap
Continuous at (a,b): f(a,b) defined, limit exists, limf=f(a,b); no hole or break in the surface. Not continuous ≠ no limit: x2+y23x2y​ has limit 0 but f(0,0) undefined.

4Partial derivatives: history, definition and notation

A partial derivative is the derivative with respect to one variable with the others held constant. The idea is already in Leibniz's product rule; the symbol ∂ came from Legendre (1786) and was reintroduced by Jacobi (1841). ∂x∂z​=zx​=fx​ is defined by a limit, and every rule of ordinary differentiation (product, quotient, chain) still holds.

Key terms and definitions

Partial derivative. A partial derivative of a function of several variables is the derivative with respect to one of those variables, with the others held constant. S001·15 · T001b 00:12:52

Formulas

E4.1 · Partial derivatives from the definitionESA ★★
∂x∂z​=h→0lim​hf(x+h,y)−f(x,y)​∂y∂z​=h→0lim​hf(x,y+h)−f(x,y)​​
giveszx​ (y held constant) and zy​ (x held constant).appliesWhen the limits exist.noteOnly one variable is moved by h; the other stays fixed.
S001·15
E4.2 · Notation for first-order partialsESA ★★
∂x∂z​=∂x∂f​=zx​=fx​,∂y∂z​=∂y∂f​=zy​=fy​
givesThe equivalent symbols.appliesz=f(x,y).noteThe symbol is ∂ (“partial”, often read “dou”), not δ or d.
S001·15 · T001b 00:11:41 · T001b 00:13:05

Flowcharts

Important points and why

  1. The product rule is already partial differentiation: in dxd​(x3sinx)=x3cosx+3x2sinx, each term treats the other factor as a constant k. Leibniz: d(uv)=udv+vdu. ESA ★ S001·14 · T001b 00:07:56 · T001b 00:10:18
  2. History: Leibniz first used partial differentiation (product rule); Adrien-Marie Legendre created the modern symbol ∂ in 1786 but later abandoned it; Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi reintroduced it in 1841. ESA ★ S001·14 · T001b 00:11:23
  3. To find zx​, look only at the terms containing x; everything else is a constant, however many other variables there are. ESA ★★ T001b 00:15:08 · T001b 00:15:48
  4. A function of x,y,t has three first partials zx​, zy​, zt​; for zx​ treat y and t as constants. ESA ★ T001b 00:13:20
  5. All rules of ordinary differentiation hold for partial derivatives: product, quotient, chain rule, implicit and composite functions. ESA ★★ T001b 00:13:57 · T001b 00:14:16
Why does every rule of ordinary differentiation still work?
With the other variables frozen, f(x,y) is an ordinary function of x alone, and ∂x∂f​ is its ordinary derivative (E4.1 is the usual limit with y fixed).
T001b 00:13:57 · S001·15
Exam trap. The partial symbol is ∂, not δ (the lecture stresses this) and not d. T001b 00:11:41

W4.1 · A partial derivative from the definitionESA ★
givenUse E4.1 to find fx​ for f(x,y)=x2y.
step 1hf(x+h,y)−f(x,y)​=h(x+h)2y−x2y​=h(2xh+h2)y​=(2x+h)y.

givenz=x3siny+ew+logp (a function of x,y,w,p). Find zx​, zp​, zy​ and zxy​.
step 1zx​: only x3siny contains x; siny is a constant: 3x2siny.
step 2zp​: only logp contains p: p1​.
step 3zy​: only siny varies: x3cosy.
step 4zxy​: differentiate zx​=3x2siny with respect to y: 3x2cosy.
answerzx​=3x2siny, zp​=p1​, zy​=x3cosy, zxy​=3x2cosy

T001b 00:14:40 · T001b 00:15:48 · T001b 00:16:26 · T001b 00:16:44
short-note recap
Partial derivative: derivative in one variable, others constant. zx​=limh→0​hf(x+h,y)−f(x,y)​; notation ∂x∂z​=zx​=fx​. Leibniz (product rule), Legendre 1786, Jacobi 1841. All differentiation rules hold.

5Second-order and mixed partial derivatives

Differentiating again gives zxx​, zyy​ and the mixed partials zxy​, zyx​. Clairaut's theorem: if the second derivatives are continuous, the order of differentiation does not matter, zxy​=zyx​. Subscripts are read in the order of differentiation; in the ∂ notation the order is read from right to left.

Key terms and definitions

Mixed (crossed) partial derivatives. zxy​=∂y∂​(∂x∂z​) and zyx​=∂x∂​(∂y∂z​): differentiate with respect to one variable, then the other. S001·16 · T001b 00:18:24
“Note 1: The crossed or mixed partial derivatives are in general equal (Clairaut's theorem): ∂x∂​(∂y∂z​)=∂y∂​(∂x∂z​). That is, the order of differentiation is immaterial if the second order derivatives involved are continuous.” S001·17 · T001b 00:19:57
“Note 2: In the subscript notation, the subscripts are written in same order in which the differentiation is carried out, while in the ∂ notation the order is opposite. For example, ∂y∂x∂2z​=∂y∂​(∂x∂z​)=fxy​.” S001·17

Formulas

zxx​=∂x∂​(∂x∂z​)=∂x2∂2z​=fxx​,zyy​=∂y∂​(∂y∂z​)=∂y2∂2z​=fyy​
givesSecond derivatives in one variable.appliesDifferentiate zx​ again in x (or zy​ in y).noteSame rules as ordinary second derivatives.
S001·16 · T001b 00:17:04
E5.2 · Mixed partialsESA ★★
zxy​=∂y∂​(∂x∂z​)=∂y∂x∂2z​=fxy​,zyx​=∂x∂​(∂y∂z​)=∂x∂y∂2z​=fyx​
givesThe two crossed derivatives.appliesDifferentiate in one variable, then the other.noteSubscripts: left to right. ∂ notation: right to left.
S001·16 · S001·17 · T001b 00:18:41
E5.3 · Clairaut's theoremESA ★★★
fxy​=fyx​(∂y∂x∂2f​=∂x∂y∂2f​)
givesThe order of differentiation does not matter.appliesfxy​ and fyx​ continuous near the point.noteCalled “a very important theorem” in the lecture; it is why Taylor's series has 2hkfxy​.
S001·17 · T001b 00:19:57 · T001b 00:20:10

Flowcharts

Important points and why

  1. Read zxyxx​ left to right: z→zx​→zxy​→zxyx​→zxyxx​ (differentiate in x, then y, then x, then x). ESA ★ T001b 00:18:51 · T001b 00:19:21
  2. Clairaut's theorem is “a very important theorem”: whenever the second partials are continuous (true for all examination functions away from bad points), compute whichever mixed partial is easier. ESA ★★★ S001·17 · T001b 00:20:10
  3. Verifying fxy​=fyx​ is a standard class-work question: xy (CW P2) and x2tan−1xy​−y2tan−1yx​ (CW P8, W5.3). ESA ★★ CW U1 P2 · CW U1 P8
Exam trap. ∂y∂x∂2z​ means x first, then y: it is zxy​, not zyx​. S001·17
Exam trap. Clairaut needs continuous second partials: for f=x2+y2xy(x2−y2)​, f(0,0)=0, one gets fxy​(0,0)=−1 but fyx​(0,0)=1. added for clarity S001·17

Worked examples

W5.1 · Second-order partials of a function of three variablesESA ★★
givenIf f(x,y,z)=ex2+y2+z2, find fxx​, fyy​, fzz​ at (−1,1,−1).
step 1fx​=2xex2+y2+z2.
step 2fxx​=(2+4x2)ex2+y2+z2 (product rule).
step 3At (−1,1,−1): x2+y2+z2=3, so fxx​=6e3; by symmetry fyy​=(2+4y2)e3=6e3, fzz​=6e3.
answerfxx​=fyy​=fzz​=6e3
checkCW answer agrees; sympy agrees.
CW U1 P4
W5.2 · Find n so that v satisfies an equationESA ★★
givenFind n so that v=rn(3cos2θ−1) satisfies ∂r∂​(r2∂r∂v​)+sinθ1​∂θ∂​(sinθ∂θ∂v​)=0.
step 1vr​=nrn−1(3cos2θ−1), so ∂r∂​(r2vr​)=n(n+1)rn(3cos2θ−1).
step 2vθ​=−6rncosθsinθ, so sinθvθ​=−6rncosθsin2θ.
step 3∂θ∂​(⋅)=−6rn(2sinθcos2θ−sin3θ); divide by sinθ: −6rn(3cos2θ−1).
step 4Sum: [n(n+1)−6]rn(3cos2θ−1)=0⇒n2+n−6=0.
answern=2 or n=−3
checkCW answer (−3, 2) agrees; sympy solves to [−3,2]. Same pattern as ESA Jan-24 s4 1c (worked in the class 002 pack).
CW U1 P7 · ESA Jan-24 s4 1c
W5.3 · Verify that the mixed partials are equalESA ★★
givenIf u=x2tan−1xy​−y2tan−1yx​, show that ∂x∂y∂2u​=∂y∂x∂2u​=x2+y2x2−y2​.
step 1ux​=2xtan−1xy​+x2⋅x2+y2−y​−y2⋅x2+y2y​=2xtan−1xy​−y.
step 2uxy​=∂y∂​(ux​)=x2+y22x2​−1=x2+y2x2−y2​.
step 3Similarly uy​=x−2ytan−1yx​, and uyx​=1−x2+y22y2​=x2+y2x2−y2​.
answeruxy​=uyx​=x2+y2x2−y2​
checksympy: both simplify to x2+y2x2−y2​.

short-note recap
zxx​, zyy​, zxy​=∂y∂​(zx​)=∂y∂x∂2z​, zyx​. Clairaut: zxy​=zyx​ when the second partials are continuous. Subscripts left to right, ∂ right to left.

Eight past ESA papers were checked: UE22MA141A Dec 2023, Jul 2023 and May 2024, and UE23MA141A Jan 2024 sets 1–4 and June 2024. No question asks for a limit, continuity or the definition of a partial derivative. Computing partial derivatives is asked directly twice: Dec 2023 Q1.a (third-order partials of exlogy+cosylogx) and Jan 2024 set 4 Q1.c (find n for θ=tne−r2/4t). Both are worked in the class 002 pack; this pack works the class-work problems of the same type (CW P4, P7, P8). Every other Unit 1 question (chain rule, Euler, Taylor, maxima and minima, Lagrange) uses the rules of this session.

Known gaps, conflicts and corrections

  1. Slide 001·9 asks for lim(x,y)→(2,1)​(x2−2xy+3y2−4x+3y−6), which is −8. The lecture (T001a 00:12:59) works the point (2,−1) instead and gets −6. Both values are correct for their points (sympy); W2.1 gives both.
  2. Slide 001·12's text is about f=x2+y23x2y​ (whose limit at the origin is 0), but the Gnuplot caption on the slide's picture reads y2+x23xy​, a different function whose limit at the origin does not exist (along y=mx it is 1+m23m​). Figure G3.1 redraws the function in the text.
  3. Slide 001·12 says the function is not continuous at (0,0) “as f(0,0) is not defined”. Added for clarity: the limit is 0, so defining f(0,0)=0 removes the discontinuity (a removable discontinuity); with 2xy/(3x2+y2) (slide 001·13) no value of f(0,0) helps.
  4. The lecture says a function is continuous “if the surface is smooth” (T001b 00:06:26). Continuity only needs no holes or jumps; a continuous surface can have a sharp edge or corner (z=∣x∣+∣y∣). Corrected as an exam trap.
  5. Slide 001·17 says mixed partials “are in general equal”. Precisely, Clairaut's theorem needs fxy​ and fyx​ continuous near the point; the standard counter-example x2+y2xy(x2−y2)​ has fxy​(0,0)=−1=fyx​(0,0)=1 (added for clarity; sympy).
  6. The lecture asks the class to prove Clairaut's theorem (T001b 00:20:10) and says the proof is short. The proof needs the mean value theorem as well as the limit definition; it is not on the slides and is not reproduced here.
  7. The lecture's history (T001b 00:10:53) says Leibniz used other letters for partial derivatives in a letter to L'Hôpital. The letters are not on the slide and could not be confirmed from the material; only the slide's facts (Leibniz, Legendre 1786, Jacobi 1841) are kept.
  8. The lecture's example function (T001a, T001b 00:15:16) adds a term in t that the recognition renders unclearly; W4.2 keeps the clearly spoken terms x3siny+ew+logp, which show the same point.
  9. The lecture opens with “Unit Two” (T001a 00:00:01); partial differentiation is Unit 1 of UE26MA141A.
  10. The deck's motivation slides (001·5–7) carry stock images (a cathode-ray tube, a weather chart, COVID-19 posters); they are described in words, not redrawn.
  11. Transcript recognition errors were corrected silently: “Clydoids” → Clairaut's, “legendary” → Legendre, “Lobithal” → L'Hôpital, “Ebo” → above, “parable” → parabola, “cathode ratio” → cathode-ray tube, “dou” / “Do” → ∂, “x q” / “XQ” → x3, “sine 1” → siny, “topol o topography” → topography, “extending to” → x tending to.
